atomic_requirement:
Article 1 — Subject-matter and objectives: Sets rules protecting natural persons regarding personal-data processing and the free movement of such
data. Protects fundamental rights, especially the right to data protection. Free movement of personal data
within the Union may not be restricted on data-protection grounds.

Article 2 — Material scope: Applies to personal data processed wholly/partly by automated means, and to manual processing that is
or will be part of a filing system. Does not apply to: processing outside the scope of Union law; Member
States' common-foreign-and-security-policy activities; purely personal/household activity; or competent
authorities' crime-prevention/investigation/prosecution processing (covered by separate instruments).

EU-institution processing is governed by Regulation (EC) 45/2001, which is to be aligned with GDPR
(Art. 98).

Article 3 — Territorial scope: Applies to processing by a controller/processor established in the Union, regardless of where the
processing itself occurs. Also applies to non-EU controllers/processors processing EU data subjects' data
where the activity relates to (a) offering goods/services to those subjects, or (b) monitoring their
behaviour within the EU. Also applies where Member State law applies under public international law.

Article 4 — Definitions: Key defined terms used throughout: personal data – any info relating to an identified/identifiable
natural person; processing – any operation on personal data (collection, storage, use, disclosure,
erasure, etc.); restriction of processing – marking stored data to limit future use; profiling –
automated evaluation of personal aspects (performance, health, preferences, location, etc.);
pseudonymisation – processing so data can't be linked to a subject without separately-held extra info;
filing system – a structured, accessible set of personal data; controller – decides purposes/means of
processing; processor – processes data on the controller's behalf; recipient – anyone data is disclosed
to; third party – anyone other than the subject, controller, processor, or their authorised staff; consent
– freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous agreement via clear affirmative action; personal data
breach – a security breach causing accidental/unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, or unauthorised
disclosure/access; genetic data, biometric data, data concerning health – special categories tied
to physical/genetic/biometric/health characteristics; main establishment – place of central EU
administration (or wherever key processing decisions are made/implemented); representative – the
EU-based contact designated under Art. 27; enterprise / group of undertakings – economic-activity
entities and their corporate groupings; binding corporate rules – intra-group international-transfer
policies; supervisory authority and supervisory authority concerned – national regulators and
those affected by a given case; cross-border processing – processing spanning establishments or
substantially affecting subjects in more than one Member State; relevant and reasoned objection –
a formal objection to a draft regulator decision showing significant risk; information society service
and international organisation – as defined in the referenced EU instruments/international law.
CHAPTER II — Principles (Articles 5–11)

article_title: Principles relating to processing of personal data
atomic_requirement:
Article 5 — Principles relating to processing of personal data: Personal data must be: (a) processed lawfully, fairly, transparently; (b) collected for specified, explicit,
legitimate purposes and not further processed incompatibly (archiving/research/statistics uses are not
automatically incompatible); (c) adequate, relevant, and limited to what's necessary (data minimisation);
(d) accurate and kept up to date; (e) kept identifiable no longer than necessary (storage limitation,
subject to the archiving exception); (f) processed with appropriate security (integrity and confidentiality).
The controller is responsible for, and must be able to demonstrate, compliance with all of the above
(accountability).

Article 6 — Lawfulness of processing: Processing is lawful only if at least one applies: (a) consent; (b) necessary for a contract with the data
subject; (c) necessary for a legal obligation; (d) necessary to protect vital interests; (e) necessary for a
public-interest/official-authority task; (f) necessary for legitimate interests not overridden by the
subject's rights (unavailable to public authorities acting in their official tasks). Member States may add
specificity for grounds (c)/(e). Where processing shifts to a new purpose without a fresh legal basis,
compatibility must be assessed against factors like the link to the original purpose, context, data
sensitivity, consequences for the subject, and safeguards in place.

Article 7 — Conditions for consent: Controllers must be able to demonstrate consent was given. Consent requests must be clearly
distinguishable, in plain language, and separate from other matters. Subjects can withdraw consent
anytime, as easily as it was given, without affecting the lawfulness of prior processing. "Freely given"
assessments must weigh whether contract performance was made conditional on consent to processing
not actually necessary for that contract.

article_title: Conditions applicable to a child's consent for information society services
atomic_requirement:
Article 8 — Conditions applicable to a child's consent for information society services: Processing based on a child's own consent is lawful from age 16; below that, parental/guardian
authorisation is required (Member States may lower the threshold to no less than 13). Controllers must
make reasonable efforts to verify parental consent given available technology. Doesn't override Member
States' general contract law on validity/formation involving a child.

article_title: Processing of special categories of personal data
atomic_requirement:
Article 9 — Processing of special categories of personal data: Processing revealing racial/ethnic origin, political opinions, religious/philosophical beliefs, trade union
membership, genetic data, biometric data used for unique ID, health data, or sex-life/orientation data is
prohibited by default. Permitted only under specific exceptions: explicit consent; employment/social-
security-law necessity; vital-interest necessity; a not-for-profit body's legitimate activities toward its own
members; data manifestly made public by the subject; legal-claims necessity; substantial public interest
(with proportionate legal basis); preventive/occupational medicine and health/social care; public-health
necessity; or archiving/research/statistics purposes. Some grounds require added safeguards (e.g.,
professional-secrecy obligations); Member States may add further conditions for
genetic/biometric/health data.

article_title: Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences
atomic_requirement:
Article 10 — Processing of personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences: Permitted only under official-authority control, or when authorised by Union/Member State law with
appropriate safeguards. Comprehensive conviction registers may only be kept under official-authority
control.

article_title: Processing which does not require identification
atomic_requirement:
Article 11 — Processing which does not require identification: Controllers aren't obliged to acquire/retain identifying information solely to comply with GDPR if they
don't otherwise need it. If a controller can show it genuinely can't identify a subject, it must say so; in that
case the access/rectification/erasure/etc. rights (Arts. 15–20) don't apply unless the subject provides
additional info enabling identification.

CHAPTER III — Rights of the data subject (Articles 12–23)
Section 1 — Transparency and modalities

Article 12 — Transparent information, communication and modalities: Controllers must provide the Art. 13/14 information and handle Art. 15–22/34 requests concisely,
transparently, intelligibly, and in plain language (with extra care for children). Generally free of charge,
though a reasonable fee or refusal is allowed for manifestly unfounded/excessive (e.g., repetitive)
requests — the controller bears the burden of proving that. Must act within one month (extendable by
two months for complex/numerous requests, with notice of the extension and reasons); must inform the
subject within one month if it won't act, including the reasons and complaint/remedy options. May
request extra identity-verification info where reasonable doubt exists. Standardised icons may
supplement (not replace) the required information.
Section 2 — Information and access to personal data

article_title: Information to be provided where data is collected from the subject
atomic_requirement:
Article 13 — Information to be provided where data is collected from the subject: At collection, controllers must disclose: controller/representative identity and contact; DPO contact;
purposes and legal basis; the legitimate interest pursued (if relying on Art. 6(1)(f)); recipients; any third-
country transfer and its safeguards; retention period/criteria; the subject's rights (access, rectification,
erasure, restriction, portability, objection, consent withdrawal, complaint to a regulator); whether
providing the data is a statutory/contractual requirement and the consequence of not providing it; and
the existence/logic/consequences of any automated decision-making. New processing purposes require
advance notice of the same kind.

article_title: Information to be provided where data was not obtained from the subject
atomic_requirement:
Article 14 — Information to be provided where data was not obtained from the subject: Same core disclosure list as Art. 13, plus the categories of data involved and the data's source. Must be
given within a reasonable time (max one month), or at first contact with the subject, or at first disclosure
to another recipient — whichever is soonest applicable. Exceptions apply where the subject already has
the info, providing it is impossible or disproportionately effortful (particularly for
archiving/research/statistics, subject to safeguards), disclosure is legally mandated with its own
protective measures, or the data must stay confidential under a professional-secrecy obligation.

article_title: Right of access by the data subject
atomic_requirement:
Article 15 — Right of access by the data subject: Subjects can confirm whether their data is being processed and, if so, access it plus: purposes, data
categories, recipients (especially international ones), retention period/criteria, their rights, the data's
source (if not collected from them), and automated decision-making logic/consequences. International
transfers trigger a right to be informed of the applicable safeguards. Controllers must provide the first
copy free; further copies may carry a reasonable administrative fee; electronic requests get an electronic
response by default. The right cannot adversely affect others' rights and freedoms.

Section 3 — Rectification and erasure

Article 16 — Right to rectification: Subjects can have inaccurate data corrected without undue delay, and incomplete data completed
(including via a supplementary statement).

article_title: Right to erasure ("right to be forgotten")
atomic_requirement:
Article 17 — Right to erasure ("right to be forgotten"): Controllers must erase data without undue delay where: it's no longer necessary for its original purpose;
consent is withdrawn with no other legal basis; the subject successfully objects (Art. 21); processing was
unlawful; erasure is a legal obligation; or the data was collected from a child regarding information
society services. If the data was made public, the controller must take reasonable steps (accounting for
cost/technology) to inform other controllers processing it that erasure of links/copies has been
requested. Exceptions: freedom of expression/information; legal obligation or public-interest/official-
authority tasks; public-health grounds (Art. 9(2)(h)/(i)); archiving/research/statistics where erasure
would seriously impair the purpose; and legal claims.

Article 18 — Right to restriction of processing: Available where: accuracy is contested (pending verification); processing is unlawful but the subject
prefers restriction over erasure; the controller no longer needs the data but the subject needs it for legal
claims; or an Art. 21 objection is pending verification. Restricted data may only be stored, or otherwise
processed with consent, for legal claims, to protect others' rights, or for important public interest. The
subject must be told before a restriction is lifted.

article_title: Notification obligation regarding rectification, erasure or restriction
atomic_requirement:
Article 19 — Notification obligation regarding rectification, erasure or restriction: Controllers must notify every recipient the data was disclosed to of any rectification, erasure, or
restriction, unless impossible or disproportionately effortful, and must tell the subject who those
recipients were if asked.

Article 20 — Right to data portability: Where processing is based on consent or contract and carried out by automated means, subjects can
receive their provided data in a structured, machine-readable format and transmit it to another
controller — directly between controllers where technically feasible. Without prejudice to Art. 17; doesn't
apply to public-interest/official-authority processing; can't adversely affect others' rights.
Section 4 — Right to object and automated individual decision-making

Article 21 — Right to object: Subjects can object anytime, on grounds relating to their particular situation, to processing based on
public-interest/official-authority or legitimate-interest grounds (Art. 6(1)(e)/(f)), including related
profiling — the controller must stop unless it demonstrates compelling overriding legitimate grounds, or
the processing is for legal claims. Objection to direct marketing (including related profiling) is
absolute — processing for that purpose must stop immediately. The right must be explicitly and

separately flagged at first contact. For information-society services, it can be exercised via automated
technical means. For research/statistics, subjects can object on particular-situation grounds unless the
processing is necessary for a public-interest task.

Article 22 — Automated individual decision-making, including profiling: Subjects have the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing (including
profiling) that produces legal or similarly significant effects, except where: necessary for a contract;
authorised by law with safeguards; or based on explicit consent. Where the contract or consent exception
applies, the controller must provide safeguards including human intervention, the right to express a view,
and the right to contest the decision. Such decisions can't be based on special-category data unless
explicit consent or a substantial-public-interest ground applies, with safeguards.
Section 5 — Restrictions

Article 23 — Restrictions: Union/Member State law may restrict the scope of the Art. 12–22 and Art. 34 rights (and the related
parts of Art. 5) via a legislative measure that respects the essence of fundamental rights and is
necessary/proportionate to safeguard things like national security, defence, public security, crime
prevention/investigation/prosecution, other important public interests
(economic/financial/monetary/tax/public-health/social-security), judicial independence, ethics-breach
investigations for regulated professions, related monitoring/inspection/regulatory functions, protecting
the subject or others' rights, or civil-claim enforcement. Any such measure must specify its purposes, the
data categories covered, its scope, anti-abuse safeguards, the responsible controller(s), storage/safeguard
periods, the risks involved, and the subject's right to be informed of the restriction (unless that would
undermine its purpose).
CHAPTER IV — Controller and processor (Articles 24–43)
Section 1 — General obligations

Article 24 — Responsibility of the controller: Controllers must implement, and keep updated, appropriate technical/organisational measures to ensure
and demonstrate GDPR-compliant processing, proportionate to the processing's
nature/scope/context/risk — potentially including formal data-protection policies. Adherence to codes of
conduct or certification can help demonstrate compliance.

article_title: Data protection by design and by default
atomic_requirement:
Article 25 — Data protection by design and by default: Controllers must build data-protection principles (e.g., minimisation, pseudonymisation) into processing
design from the outset, and ensure that, by default, only the personal data necessary for each specific
purpose is processed — covering the amount collected, the extent of processing, storage duration, and

accessibility. By default, data shouldn't be made accessible to an indefinite number of people without the
individual's action. Certification can help demonstrate compliance.

Article 26 — Joint controllers: Where two or more controllers jointly determine the purposes/means of processing, they must
transparently allocate their respective responsibilities (especially for subject-rights handling and Art.
13/14 disclosures) via an arrangement, unless law already determines this — the essence of that
arrangement must be made available to subjects. Subjects may exercise their rights against either or both
controllers regardless of the arrangement's internal terms.

Article 27 — Representatives of non-EU controllers/processors: Where Art. 3(2) applies, a written-designated EU representative is required, based in a Member State
where the relevant data subjects are, and mandated to be the point of contact for regulators and subjects.
Exempt for occasional, small-scale, low-risk processing, or for public authorities. Designating a
representative doesn't shield the controller/processor from legal action.

Article 28 — Processor: Controllers may only use processors offering sufficient guarantees. Processors can't engage a sub-
processor without prior specific or general written authorisation (with a right to object to changes under
general authorisation). Processing must be governed by a binding written contract specifying subject-
matter, duration, nature/purpose, data/subject types, and each party's obligations — requiring the
processor to: act only on documented controller instructions; ensure staff confidentiality; implement Art.
32 security; respect sub-processor conditions; help the controller respond to subject-rights requests and
meet Art. 32–36 obligations; delete/return data at contract end; and provide compliance
information/allow audits (flagging any instruction it believes is unlawful). The same obligations must
flow down to any sub-processor, with the initial processor remaining liable for the sub-processor's
failures. Commission- or regulator-approved compliance contractual clauses may be used. A processor that
oversteps into determining its own purposes/means becomes a controller for that processing.

article_title: Processing under the authority of the controller or processor
atomic_requirement:
Article 29 — Processing under the authority of the controller or processor: Anyone processing data under a controller's or processor's authority may do so only on instruction,
unless legally required otherwise.

Article 30 — Records of processing activities: Controllers (and representatives) must maintain records covering: controller/DPO contact details,
purposes, data-subject and data categories, recipient categories (including international), transfer
details/safeguards, retention time limits, and a general description of security measures. Processors must
keep an analogous record of processing categories performed for each controller. Must be in writing
(including electronic) and produced to regulators on request. Exempt for organisations under 250
employees unless the processing risks subject rights, is non-occasional, or involves special-
category/criminal data.

Article 31 — Cooperation with the supervisory authority: Controllers, processors, and their representatives must cooperate with a regulator on request.
Section 2 — Security of personal data

Article 32 — Security of processing: Controllers and processors must implement risk-appropriate technical/organisational security measures,
considering cost and context, including: pseudonymisation/encryption; ongoing confidentiality,
integrity, availability, and resilience of systems; the ability to restore access after an incident; and regular
testing/evaluation of those measures. Must account for risks like accidental/unlawful destruction, loss,
alteration, or unauthorised disclosure/access. Code-of-conduct or certification adherence can help
demonstrate compliance. Anyone under the controller's/processor's authority may only process data on
instruction, unless legally required otherwise.

article_title: Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority
atomic_requirement:
Article 33 — Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority: Controllers must notify the competent regulator without undue delay, within 72 hours where feasible,
unless the breach is unlikely to risk subjects' rights (late notice requires a justification). Processors must
notify controllers without undue delay upon becoming aware. The notification must cover: the breach's
nature (data-subject/record categories and approximate numbers); DPO/contact details; likely
consequences; and mitigation measures taken/proposed — info can be phased if not all available at once.
Controllers must document every breach (facts, effects, remedial action) so regulators can verify
compliance.

article_title: Communication of a personal data breach to the data subject
atomic_requirement:
Article 34 — Communication of a personal data breach to the data subject: Required without undue delay where a breach is likely to result in a high risk to subjects' rights,
describing the breach in plain language plus the mitigation/consequence details from Art. 33(3). Not
required if: the affected data was protected by measures like encryption; the controller has since
neutralised the high risk; or notifying individually would be disproportionately effortful (in which case a
public communication substitutes). Regulators can compel communication if the controller hasn't
already done it.
Section 3 — Data protection impact assessment and prior consultation

Article 35 — Data protection impact assessment (DPIA): Required before any processing (especially using new technologies) likely to result in high risk,
considering nature/scope/context/purpose — one assessment can cover a set of similar high-risk
operations. DPO advice must be sought where one is designated. Mandatory specifically for: systematic,
extensive automated evaluation/profiling with legal or similarly significant effects; large-scale processing
of special-category/criminal data; or large-scale systematic monitoring of public areas. Regulators must
publish (and share with the EDPB) lists of processing types requiring — or exempt from — a DPIA. A
DPIA must contain: a systematic description of the processing/purposes; a necessity/proportionality
assessment; a risk assessment; and the measures (safeguards, security, compliance mechanisms)

addressing those risks. Code-of-conduct adherence is a relevant factor. Subject/representative views
should be sought where appropriate. Exempted where an equivalent impact assessment already occurred
at the legislative stage for an Art. 6(1)(c)/(e) legal basis (unless a Member State requires otherwise). Must
be reviewed if risk changes.

Article 36 — Prior consultation: Controllers must consult their regulator before processing if a DPIA shows unmitigated high risk. If the
regulator believes the intended processing would infringe GDPR, it must give written advice within 8
weeks (extendable by 6 for complexity) and may exercise its Art. 58 powers. The controller must supply:
party responsibilities, purposes/means, planned safeguards, DPO contact, the DPIA itself, and any other
requested information. Member States must also consult regulators on relevant legislative measures, and
may require prior authorisation for certain public-interest processing.
Section 4 — Data protection officer

article_title: Designation of the data protection officer (DPO)
atomic_requirement:
Article 37 — Designation of the data protection officer (DPO): Mandatory where: the controller/processor is a public authority (except courts acting judicially); its
core activities require regular, systematic, large-scale monitoring of subjects; or its core activities involve
large-scale processing of special-category/criminal data. A shared DPO is allowed across a group of
undertakings (if easily accessible from each establishment) or across multiple public bodies. Voluntary
designation is otherwise possible (or may be required by Member State law). The DPO must be chosen
for professional quality and expert knowledge, can be internal staff or contracted, and contact details
must be published and shared with the regulator.

article_title: Position of the data protection officer
atomic_requirement:
Article 38 — Position of the data protection officer: The DPO must be involved properly and promptly in all data-protection matters, given adequate
resources/access/training support, free from instructions regarding task performance, protected from
dismissal/penalty for doing the job, and must report to the highest management level. Subjects may
contact the DPO on any related issue. The DPO is bound by confidentiality and may hold other roles only
if free of conflicts of interest.

article_title: Tasks of the data protection officer
atomic_requirement:
Article 39 — Tasks of the data protection officer: At minimum: inform/advise the organisation and staff of their obligations; monitor compliance
(including responsibility assignment, training, and audits); advise on and monitor DPIAs; cooperate with
the regulator; and act as its point of contact (including for prior consultation) — always with due regard
to processing risk.
Section 5 — Codes of conduct and certification

Article 40 — Codes of conduct: Regulators/EDPB/Commission must encourage codes of conduct, considering sector needs and those of
small/medium enterprises. Associations may draft codes covering things like fair/transparent

processing, legitimate interests, data collection, pseudonymisation, subject information, exercising
subject rights, child/parental-consent handling, Art. 24/25/32 measures, breach notification,
international transfers, and dispute resolution. Approved codes can also serve non-EU-subject
controllers as an Art. 46(2)(e) transfer safeguard via binding commitments. Codes need a compliance-
monitoring mechanism (Art. 41). Draft codes go to the competent regulator for approval (single Member
State) or through the EDPB consistency mechanism (multi-Member-State), after which the Commission
may grant them general EU-wide validity. The EDPB maintains a public code register.

article_title: Monitoring of approved codes of conduct
atomic_requirement:
Article 41 — Monitoring of approved codes of conduct: Monitoring may be delegated to an accredited body that has demonstrated independence, expertise,
eligibility/compliance-review procedures, transparent complaint-handling, and no conflict of interest —
accreditation requirements go through the EDPB consistency mechanism. Such a body can
suspend/exclude non-compliant members (informing the regulator), and its accreditation is revoked if it
stops meeting requirements or itself infringes GDPR. Doesn't apply to public-authority processing.

Article 42 — Certification: Regulators/EDPB/Commission are encouraged to establish certification mechanisms/seals/marks
demonstrating compliance, considering SME needs; approved certification can also serve as an Art. 46(2)
(f) transfer safeguard for non-EU-subject entities via binding commitments. Certification is voluntary,
transparent, doesn't reduce the controller's/processor's own compliance responsibility, and doesn't limit
regulator powers. Issued by accredited certification bodies (Art. 43) or the competent regulator, based on
approved criteria (Board-approved criteria can produce the European Data Protection Seal). Valid up to
3 years, renewable, and withdrawn if criteria are no longer met.

Article 43 — Certification bodies: Must be accredited (by the competent regulator and/or a national accreditation body under EN-ISO/IEC
17065) based on demonstrated independence/expertise, commitment to approved certification criteria,
defined issuance/review/withdrawal procedures, transparent complaint-handling, and no conflict of
interest. Responsible for proper certification assessments (without reducing the certified entity's own
compliance responsibility). Accreditation lasts up to 5 years, renewable, and is revoked if requirements
aren't met or the body itself infringes GDPR.
CHAPTER V — Transfers of personal data to third countries or
international organisations (Articles 44–50)

chapter_title: Transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations
atomic_requirement:
Article 44 — General principle for transfers: Any transfer (including onward transfers) to a third country or international organisation must satisfy
this Chapter's conditions, to ensure GDPR's protection level isn't undermined.

chapter_title: Transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations
article_title: Transfers on the basis of an adequacy decision
atomic_requirement:
Article 45 — Transfers on the basis of an adequacy decision: Permitted without specific authorisation where the Commission has decided the destination
country/sector/organisation ensures adequate protection — assessed via rule of law, relevant legislation
and enforcement, effective independent regulator(s), and relevant international commitments. Adopted
via implementing act with periodic review (at least every four years); the Commission must monitor
ongoing developments and can amend/suspend/repeal the decision (including via an urgency procedure)
if adequacy lapses, and must publish the current adequacy list. Loss of adequacy doesn't block transfers
made instead under Arts. 46–49.

chapter_title: Transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations
atomic_requirement:
Article 46 — Transfers subject to appropriate safeguards: Absent an adequacy decision, transfers are allowed with appropriate safeguards plus enforceable
rights/remedies for subjects. No specific regulator authorisation needed for: binding public-authority
instruments; binding corporate rules (Art. 47); Commission-adopted or regulator-adopted/Commission-
approved compliance contractual clauses; an approved code of conduct with binding commitments; or
approved certification with binding commitments. Regulator authorisation is needed for ad hoc
contractual clauses or administrative arrangements between public bodies with enforceable rights.

chapter_title: Transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations
atomic_requirement:
Article 47 — Binding corporate rules (BCRs): Approved by the competent regulator via the EDPB consistency mechanism, provided the rules are
legally binding group-wide (including for employees), grant subjects enforceable rights, and specify:
group structure/contacts; the data/transfers covered; their binding nature; how GDPR principles are
applied; subject rights and how to exercise them; the EU member's liability for non-EU members'
breaches; how subjects are informed; the compliance-monitoring role (DPO or equivalent); complaint
procedures; audit/verification mechanisms; change-reporting mechanisms; the regulator-cooperation
mechanism; reporting of conflicting third-country legal demands; and staff training.

chapter_title: Transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations
article_title: Transfers or disclosures not authorised by Union law
atomic_requirement:
Article 48 — Transfers or disclosures not authorised by Union law: A foreign court/authority order to transfer or disclose data is only recognisable/enforceable if grounded
in an international agreement (e.g., a mutual legal assistance treaty) between the requesting country and
the EU/Member State — without prejudice to other Chapter V transfer grounds.

chapter_title: Transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations
atomic_requirement:
Article 49 — Derogations for specific situations: Absent an adequacy decision or Art. 46 safeguards, transfers are only allowed where: the subject gave
explicit, risk-informed consent to that specific transfer; it's necessary for contract performance/pre-
contractual steps; necessary for a contract in the subject's interest; necessary for important public-
interest reasons; necessary for legal claims; necessary to protect vital interests where consent is
impossible; or made from a public register under its normal access conditions (not covering the register
wholesale). Failing all of those, a narrow residual derogation permits non-repetitive, limited-scope
transfers necessary for compelling controller interests not overridden by the subject's rights — requiring
a documented risk assessment, suitable safeguards, and notice to both the regulator and the data subject.

chapter_title: Transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations
article_title: International cooperation for the protection of personal data
atomic_requirement:
Article 50 — International cooperation for the protection of personal data: The Commission and regulators must work to build international enforcement-cooperation mechanisms,
provide mutual assistance, engage relevant stakeholders, and promote the exchange of data-protection
law/practice, including on cross-border jurisdictional conflicts.
CHAPTER VI — Independent supervisory authorities (Articles
51–59)
(Chapter VI governs how national data-protection regulators are structured and empowered — mostly
relevant to regulators rather than to company policies, condensed accordingly.)
Section 1 — Independent status

Article 51 — Supervisory authority: Each Member State must establish one or more independent regulators to monitor GDPR compliance
and support free data flow, cooperating with each other under Chapter VII; multi-regulator states must
designate a single EDPB representative.

Article 52 — Independence: Regulators must act with complete independence, free of outside instruction, with adequate resources,
independent staff, and financial controls that don't compromise that independence.

Article 53 — General conditions for members: Members are appointed via a transparent procedure (parliament, government, head of state, or an
independent body), must have relevant qualifications, and can only be dismissed for serious misconduct
or failure to meet eligibility conditions.

Article 54 — Rules on establishment: Member States must legislate on establishment, member qualifications, appointment procedures, term
length (at least four years, with a staggered-first-term exception), reappointment rules, and conduct
obligations; members/staff are bound by professional secrecy.
Section 2 — Competence, tasks and powers

Article 55 — Competence: Regulators are competent within their own Member State, with a special rule for certain public-authority
processing; courts acting judicially are outside regulator supervision.

article_title: Competence of the lead supervisory authority
atomic_requirement:
Article 56 — Competence of the lead supervisory authority: For cross-border processing, the regulator where the controller/processor has its main/single EU
establishment acts as lead authority, following the Art. 60 cooperation procedure — with an exception
allowing a purely local regulator to handle matters affecting only its own territory/subjects, subject to
lead-authority sign-off.

Article 57 — Tasks: Includes enforcing GDPR, raising public/child awareness, advising government, informing subjects of
their rights, handling and investigating complaints, cooperating with other regulators, conducting
investigations, adopting compliance contractual clauses, maintaining DPIA-requirement lists, approving
codes of conduct/certification criteria, accrediting monitoring/certification bodies, approving BCRs, and
contributing to the EDPB — generally free of charge to the complainant (fees/refusal allowed for
unfounded or excessive requests).

Article 58 — Powers: Investigative: order information, conduct audits, review certifications, access data/premises.
Corrective: warn, reprimand, order compliance with subject-rights requests or with GDPR generally,
order breach communication, impose processing bans/limits, order rectification/erasure/restriction,
withdraw certification, impose administrative fines (Art. 83), suspend third-country data flows.
Authorisation/advisory: advise on prior consultation, issue public opinions, authorise
processing/clauses/arrangements, approve codes of conduct/certification/BCRs. All subject to judicial-
remedy and due-process safeguards; regulators must also be able to refer infringements to courts.

Article 59 — Activity reports: Regulators must publish annual activity reports, shared with national bodies, the Commission, and the
EDPB.
CHAPTER VII — Cooperation and consistency (Articles 60–76)
(Chapter VII governs how national regulators and the EDPB coordinate on cross-border cases — inter-
regulator process, condensed heavily as it rarely constrains a company's own policies directly.)
Section 1 — Cooperation

article_title: Cooperation between the lead and concerned supervisory authorities
atomic_requirement:
Article 60 — Cooperation between the lead and concerned supervisory authorities: The lead regulator must share information and draft decisions with other "concerned" regulators, aim for
consensus, and take their views into account; unresolved reasoned objections escalate to the Art. 63
consistency mechanism. Final decisions are formally notified to the controller/processor and other
regulators/EDPB/complainants, with the controller/processor required to report back on compliance
measures taken.

Article 61 — Mutual assistance: Regulators must provide each other relevant information and assistance (info requests, inspections,
investigations) within about a month, usable only for its stated purpose; refusal is allowed only for lack of
competence or legal conflict.

Article 62 — Joint operations: Regulators may run joint investigations/enforcement actions; participation rights and staff liability
follow the host regulator's Member State law, with cross-state liability/reimbursement rules for any
damage caused.
Section 2 — Consistency

Article 63 — Consistency mechanism: Regulators cooperate with each other and the Commission through this mechanism to keep GDPR
application consistent EU-wide.

Article 64 — Opinion of the Board: The EDPB must give an opinion before a regulator adopts certain EU-wide-impact decisions (DPIA lists,
code-of-conduct/certification approvals, compliance contractual clauses, BCR approvals), and can be asked
to weigh in on other general or multi-state matters; opinions come within about 8 weeks (extendable by
6), and the regulator must give the opinion "utmost account," reporting back on whether it will follow it.

Article 65 — Dispute resolution by the Board: The EDPB issues binding decisions to resolve unresolved reasoned objections, lead-authority
competence disputes, or a regulator's failure to follow an Art. 64 opinion — within about a month
(extendable), by a two-thirds (or fallback simple) majority, binding on all regulators involved.

Article 66 — Urgency procedure: In exceptional urgent circumstances, a regulator may adopt short-lived (max 3-month) local provisional
measures outside the normal consistency process, and may request an urgent EDPB opinion/binding
decision (turned around within 2 weeks) for final measures.

Article 67 — Exchange of information: The Commission may specify standardised electronic formats for regulator-to-regulator and regulator-to-
EDPB information exchange.
Section 3 — European Data Protection Board

Article 68 — European Data Protection Board (EDPB): An EU body with legal personality, composed of one representative per Member State regulator plus the
European Data Protection Supervisor; the Commission participates without voting rights.

Article 69 — Independence: The EDPB acts independently, without seeking or taking outside instructions (aside from Commission
requests it may act on).

Article 70 — Tasks of the Board: Ensures consistent GDPR application; advises the Commission on data-protection issues/amendments;
issues wide-ranging guidelines, recommendations, and best practices (on erasure, profiling, breach
notification/high-risk criteria, BCR requirements, international-transfer criteria, fine-setting guidance,
whistleblower procedures, etc.); approves certification criteria and maintains public registers; opines on
third-country adequacy and Union-level codes of conduct; issues Art. 64/65 opinions and binding
decisions; and promotes regulator cooperation, training, and international knowledge exchange.

Article 71 — Reports: The EDPB must publish an annual report reviewing guideline application and binding decisions, sent to
the Parliament, Council, and Commission.
Article 72 — Procedure: Decisions by simple majority unless stated otherwise; procedural rules adopted by a two-thirds majority.
Article 73 — Chair: A Chair and two deputy chairs are elected for renewable five-year terms.

Article 74 — Tasks of the Chair: Convenes meetings, sets agendas, notifies Art. 65 decisions, and ensures timely performance of the
consistency mechanism.

Article 75 — Secretariat: Provided by the European Data Protection Supervisor's office, handling day-to-day administration,
communications, translation, and drafting/publishing EDPB opinions and decisions.

Article 76 — Confidentiality: EDPB discussions may be confidential per its own procedural rules; document access follows the general
EU public-access regulation.

CHAPTER VIII — Remedies, liability and penalties (Articles 77–
84)

article_title: Right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority
atomic_requirement:
Article 77 — Right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority: Subjects can complain to a regulator (typically of their residence, workplace, or the alleged
infringement's location), without prejudice to other remedies; the regulator must keep them informed of
progress and outcome.

article_title: Right to an effective judicial remedy against a supervisory authority
atomic_requirement:
Article 78 — Right to an effective judicial remedy against a supervisory authority: Available against a binding regulator decision, or against a regulator's failure to handle/update on a
complaint within three months — brought before that regulator's own Member State courts.

article_title: Right to an effective judicial remedy against a controller or processor
atomic_requirement:
Article 79 — Right to an effective judicial remedy against a controller or processor: Available where GDPR-infringing processing has affected the subject's rights, without prejudice to the
Art. 77 complaint route — brought where the controller/processor is established, or (subject's choice)
where the subject habitually resides, except against a public authority acting officially.

Article 80 — Representation of data subjects: Subjects may mandate a qualified not-for-profit body (public-interest mission, active in the data-
protection field) to lodge complaints and exercise Arts. 77–79 rights on their behalf, and — where
Member State law allows — to claim compensation too. Member States may also let such bodies act
independently of a specific mandate.

Article 81 — Suspension of proceedings: Courts handling the same subject matter, controller, or processor as a parallel case in another Member
State must coordinate, and may suspend or (at first instance) decline jurisdiction in favour of the court
first seized.

Article 82 — Right to compensation and liability: Anyone suffering material or non-material damage from a GDPR infringement can claim compensation
from the controller or processor. Controllers are liable for infringing processing generally; processors are
liable only for breaching processor-specific obligations or acting outside/against controller instructions
— either can be exempted by proving no responsibility for the triggering event. Multiple liable parties are
jointly and severally liable to ensure the subject is fully compensated, with internal reallocation of costs
based on responsibility share afterward.

article_title: General conditions for imposing administrative fines
atomic_requirement:
Article 83 — General conditions for imposing administrative fines: Fines must be effective, proportionate, and dissuasive, weighed against factors like the infringement's
nature/gravity/duration/scope, intent vs. negligence, mitigation steps taken, technical/organisational
measures already in place, prior infringements, cooperation with the regulator, data sensitivity, how the
breach came to light (including self-reporting), and code/certification adherence. Combined

infringements from the same/linked processing are capped at the gravest infringement's maximum.
Lower tier (up to €10M or 2% global annual turnover, whichever is higher): breaches of
controller/processor obligations under Arts. 8, 11, 25–39, 42–43, plus certification/monitoring-body
obligations. Upper tier (up to €20M or 4% global annual turnover, whichever is higher): breaches of the
core principles/consent conditions (Arts. 5, 6, 7, 9), data-subject rights (Arts. 12–22), international-
transfer rules (Arts. 44–49), Chapter IX Member State-law obligations, and non-compliance with
regulator orders. Subject to judicial-remedy/due-process safeguards; Member States without
administrative fining powers use an equivalent court-based process instead.

Article 84 — Penalties: Member States must set other effective/proportionate/dissuasive penalties for infringements not covered
by Art. 83 fines, and notify the relevant provisions to the Commission.
CHAPTER IX — Provisions relating to specific processing
situations (Articles 85–91)

chapter_title: Provisions relating to specific processing situations
article_title: Processing and freedom of expression and information
atomic_requirement:
Article 85 — Processing and freedom of expression and information: Member States must reconcile data protection with freedom of expression (including journalism and
academic/artistic/literary expression) by law, providing necessary exemptions from Chapters II, III, IV,
V, VI, VII, and IX where needed.

chapter_title: Provisions relating to specific processing situations
article_title: Processing and public access to official documents
atomic_requirement:
Article 86 — Processing and public access to official documents: Personal data in official documents may be disclosed by public authorities/bodies (or private bodies
performing public-interest tasks) under Union/Member State law that reconciles public-access rules with
data protection.

chapter_title: Provisions relating to specific processing situations
article_title: Processing of the national identification number
atomic_requirement:
Article 87 — Processing of the national identification number: Member States may set specific conditions for processing national ID numbers or similar identifiers,
subject to appropriate safeguards.

chapter_title: Provisions relating to specific processing situations
article_title: Processing in the context of employment
atomic_requirement:
Article 88 — Processing in the context of employment: Member States may set more specific rules (by law or collective agreement) for employment-related
processing (recruitment, contract performance, management, equality, health & safety, property
protection, termination, etc.), including safeguards for dignity, transparency, intra-group transfers, and
workplace monitoring.

chapter_title: Provisions relating to specific processing situations
article_title: Safeguards and derogations for archiving, research and statistics
atomic_requirement:
Article 89 — Safeguards and derogations for archiving, research and statistics: Such processing requires appropriate safeguards, particularly technical/organisational measures
supporting data minimisation (e.g., pseudonymisation or non-identifying alternatives where feasible).
Union/Member State law may derogate from certain subject rights (varying slightly between the

research/statistics and archiving contexts) where those rights would seriously impair achieving the
purpose and the derogation is necessary.

chapter_title: Provisions relating to specific processing situations
atomic_requirement:
Article 90 — Obligations of secrecy: Member States may set specific rules limiting certain regulator investigative powers toward
controllers/processors bound by legal/professional secrecy, where necessary to reconcile data protection
with that secrecy obligation — limited to data received under it.

article_title: Existing data protection rules of churches and religious associations
atomic_requirement:
Article 91 — Existing data protection rules of churches and religious associations: Pre-existing comprehensive data-protection rules of churches/religious associations may continue if
aligned with GDPR, subject to supervision by an independent regulator meeting Chapter VI's conditions.
CHAPTER X — Delegated and implementing acts (Articles 92–
93)

Article 92 — Exercise of the delegation: The Commission's power to adopt delegated acts (for Art. 12(8) icons and Art. 43(8) certification
requirements) runs indefinitely from 24 May 2016, is revocable anytime by Parliament/Council
(prospectively only), and any adopted act must be notified to both bodies and only enters into force if
neither objects within three months (extendable by three more).

Article 93 — Committee procedure: The Commission is assisted by a standing committee, using compliance or urgency examination procedures
as referenced elsewhere in the Regulation.
CHAPTER XI — Final provisions (Articles 94–99)

Article 94 — Repeal of Directive 95/46/EC: The prior Data Protection Directive is repealed from 25 May 2018; references to it (and to the former Art.
29 Working Party) are read as references to GDPR (and the EDPB, respectively).

Article 95 — Relationship with Directive 2002/58/EC: GDPR doesn't add extra obligations for public electronic-communications processing already covered by
equivalent obligations under the ePrivacy Directive.

Article 96 — Relationship with previously concluded agreements: International data-transfer agreements predating 24 May 2016 that complied with prior EU law remain
valid until amended/replaced/revoked.

Article 97 — Commission reports: The Commission must report on GDPR's evaluation/review to Parliament and Council by 25 May 2020
and every four years after, focusing particularly on Chapter V (transfers) and Chapter VII
(cooperation/consistency), and may propose amendments as needed.

article_title: Review of other Union legal acts on data protection
atomic_requirement:
Article 98 — Review of other Union legal acts on data protection: The Commission must, where appropriate, propose amendments to other EU data-protection
instruments (especially covering EU institutions) to keep protection consistent.

Article 99 — Entry into force and application: Entered into force 20 days after Official Journal publication; applied from 25 May 2018; binding and
directly applicable across all Member States.
